clue.text: Measly fate for Raphael's sorcerer

indicators.note: the fate of the word measly is to be broken up and its letters set in a new order

explanation.surface: A sorry end awaits the magician in Raphael's painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fate' signals the anagram of MEASLY. Elymas is the sorcerer struck blind by St Paul, the subject of one of Raphael's tapestry cartoons.
explanation.definitionFit: Elymas the magician appears in Raphael's cartoon The Blinding of Elymas, made for Sistine Chapel tapestries.

clue.text: Uncovered by Burroughs and Monet

parts.note: uncovered means naked, as in William Burroughs's novel title, and the French painter's famous picnic scene Le Dejeuner sur l'herbe names the same midday meal

explanation.surface: Something exposed in the work of an American novelist and a French painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Burroughs wrote Naked Lunch; the painting Le Dejeuner sur l'herbe (the famous nude version is Manet's, though Monet also painted one) shows the same meal, so 'Uncovered' is the naked of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Burroughs's novel is Naked Lunch, and dejeuner in the painting's title is the French word for the midday meal.

clue.text: "And tall — catch the dying sun" (R. L. Stevenson, Underwoods)

definitions.text: "And tall — catch the dying sun" (R. L. Stevenson, Underwoods)

parts.words: "And tall — catch the dying sun" (R. L. Stevenson, Underwoods)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the one Stevenson wrote in his poetry collection Underwoods

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the solver supplies the missing word of Stevenson's line, 'And tall memorials catch the dying sun'.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation's gap is filled by the word for monuments raised in remembrance, which stand tall enough to catch late sunlight.

clue.text: River hero of Williamson in Universal moneymaker

indicators.note: in tells the solver the answer is sitting inside the words universal moneymaker

explanation.surface: A film studio's box-office hit stars Henry Williamson's river creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Williamson wrote Salar the Salmon (and Tarka the Otter); the answer lies inside 'UniverSAL MONeymaker'.
explanation.definitionFit: Salar, the hero of Henry Williamson's novel, is an Atlantic fish of that kind that swims up rivers to spawn.

clue.text: Notorious thief finds singing group going back and forth in saloons

indicators.note: in places the band's name within the word for drinking places

parts.note: saloons are bars

indicators.note: going back and forth says the band's name reads identically either way

parts.note: Abba was the Swedish pop group

explanation.surface: A notorious robber spots a pop band touring the pubs in both directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going back and forth' is only a flourish here: the band's name is a palindrome, so nothing actually needs turning round before it goes into the saloons.
explanation.definitionFit: Barabbas was the robber released by Pilate in place of Jesus, according to the Gospels.

clue.text: Beach much in demand in heavy weather here

definitions.text: Beach much in demand in heavy weather here

parts.words: Beach much in demand in heavy weather here
parts.note: Beach is not the seaside but Lord Emsworth's butler in P. G. Wodehouse, and Heavy Weather is one of the novels set at the Earl's Shropshire home

explanation.surface: A seaside spot is popular when storms roll in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beach' looks like sand and sea; it is Wodehouse's butler Beach, and 'Heavy Weather' is a Wodehouse novel title, so 'here' is the ancestral seat where both are found.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of Emsworth's seat in Wodehouse's novels is where the butler Beach serves and where Heavy Weather is set.

clue.text: Observation heard from war novelist

indicators.note: heard means the word for an observation is spoken, giving a surname with the same pronunciation

parts.note: an observation is a remark

explanation.surface: A comment overheard from a writer about war.
explanation.walkthrough: Erich Maria Remarque wrote All Quiet on the Western Front.
explanation.definitionFit: Erich Maria Remarque wrote All Quiet on the Western Front, the classic First World War novel.

clue.text: One of the "caterpillars of the commonwealth to acquire book

definitions.text: One of the "caterpillars of the commonwealth

parts.note: to bag something is to acquire it
OT, the Old Testament, is a book of scripture

explanation.surface: One of Shakespeare's parasites of the realm sets out to obtain a volume.
explanation.walkthrough: In Richard II, Bolingbroke calls Bushy, Bagot and Green 'the caterpillars of the commonwealth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir William Bagot is one of the three favourites of Richard II whom Bolingbroke denounces as parasites in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: It may have provided turnover for Shaw

definitions.text: It may have provided turnover for Shaw

parts.words: It may have provided turnover for Shaw
parts.note: a turnover is a pastry filled with fruit, but also an upset; Shaw wrote a political comedy titled after the cart whose upsetting is proverbial

explanation.surface: Something that might have supplied pastries or business for a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's play is The Apple Cart; an apple turnover is a pastry, and to upset the cart is to overturn plans.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's 1928 political play takes its title from the barrow whose upsetting means ruining a plan.

clue.text: Napoleon demanded windmills here (649)

parts.note: Napoleon is not the French emperor but Orwell's tyrant pig, who has the other beasts build a windmill on the farm

explanation.surface: The French emperor called for wind power somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Napoleon' suggests Bonaparte; he is the pig who rules in Orwell's fable and forces the animals to rebuild the windmill.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's allegory is set on a farm run by pigs, where the boar Napoleon has the beasts labour on a windmill.

clue.text: Stare at torn page

indicators.note: a torn page is ripped up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone gazes at a ripped page of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: To gape is to stare open-mouthed in wonder.

clue.text: Whose rod broken here? Little John's?

indicators.note: broken tells the solver the letters of whose rod are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Asking whose fishing rod was snapped in the forest: Little John's?
explanation.walkthrough: Little John is Robin Hood's lieutenant; 'here' points to their forest home.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood's band, Little John among them, lived in the Nottinghamshire forest, so it is his haunt.

clue.text: River hero of Williamson is a cad

parts.note: Henry Williamson wrote Tarka the Otter

explanation.surface: The river creature in Williamson's novel is a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotter is an old-fashioned British word for a contemptible scoundrel.

clue.text: A festival for Dali

definitions.meaning: a festive celebration or special occasion
The Russian-born wife and muse of the painter Salvador Dali

explanation.surface: A celebration held in honour of the Spanish surrealist.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive occasion, and Gala was the name of Salvador Dali's wife and muse.

clue.text: Quasi-black haircut, say, tied differently for deity

indicators.note: say signals the hairstyle's name is taken by its pronunciation and spelt another way

parts.note: an Afro is a hairstyle associated with Black people

indicators.note: differently means the letters of tied are arranged another way

explanation.surface: A goddess with something like an Afro, tied up in a new style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' turns AFRO into APHRO by sound; 'differently' makes DITE from TIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphrodite is the Greek goddess of love and beauty.

clue.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

definitions.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

parts.words: Odysseus heard that she played ball
parts.note: in Homer, the shipwrecked hero is woken by the cries of a princess and her maids playing ball on the shore

explanation.surface: The Greek hero learned that a girl played ball games.
explanation.walkthrough: In Odyssey Book 6 Odysseus, asleep on Scheria, is woken by the shout when the princess's ball falls into the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phaeacian princess in Homer's Odyssey is playing ball with her maids when the shipwrecked hero wakes.

clue.text: Polo record, perhaps

parts.note: Polo is not the horseback sport but Marco Polo, whose book recorded his route across Asia

explanation.surface: A record of a match in the horseback sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polo' suggests the game; it is the Venetian traveller Marco Polo, whose Travels is an account of his journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco Polo's Travels records his route, the kind of account of a journey that a travel plan or log provides.

clue.text: A follower of George MacDonald

definitions.meaning: an adherent or pupil of a teacher
the Scottish writer George MacDonald published The ... and Other Poems

explanation.surface: Someone who follows the Victorian Scottish fantasy writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is an adherent of a teacher, and The Disciple is the title of a poem collection by George MacDonald.

clue.text: I was below par to the extent of two —(C. E. Montague, Fiery Particles)

definitions.text: I was below par to the extent of two —(C. E. Montague, Fiery Particles)

parts.words: I was below par to the extent of two —(C. E. Montague, Fiery Particles)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Montague's story collection, the gap being drinks of Scotch

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the solver completes Montague's line, the missing word being the spirit drinks the speaker was short of.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names glasses of distilled Scotch spirit, the shortfall that left the speaker feeling below par.

clue.text: Small-part of Cassio taken by grateful actor

indicators.note: of tells the solver the answer is a part taken out of the words Cassio taken

explanation.surface: A grateful actor accepts a minor role as Cassio in Othello.
explanation.walkthrough: Cassio is Othello's lieutenant; the answer is hidden in 'CassIO TAken'.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota is the smallest Greek letter, hence a tiny amount or a very small part.

clue.text: Laureates verse, suggesting Tennyson

parts.note: Tennyson's first name was shared by Austin, his successor as Poet Laureate

explanation.surface: The poetry of the official poets brings Tennyson to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Tennyson and Alfred Austin were successive Poets Laureate, so the laureates' verse suggests that shared first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson and Alfred Austin were successive Poets Laureate, sharing that first name.

clue.text: Law governing floor design?

definitions.meaning: the law of Moses, the code governing Israel in the Old Testament
a pattern of small tiles or stones laid in a floor

explanation.surface: Rules covering the pattern of a floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mosaic law is the law of Moses, and a floor pattern made of small tiles or tesserae is the art form of the same name.

clue.text: An opening for a critic

parts.note: a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: An opportunity for a reviewer.
explanation.walkthrough: James Agate was a famous British theatre critic of the 1920s to 1940s.
explanation.definitionFit: James Agate was the long-serving drama critic of the Sunday Times.

clue.text: Everyone at Suffolk town, including English thriller writer

parts.note: everyone means all

indicators.note: including says the town's name takes the abbreviation for English inside it

parts.note: Bury St Edmunds, often just Bury, is a town in Suffolk in eastern England

explanation.surface: Everyone in a Suffolk town, including an English writer of thrillers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ted Allbeury was a British spy novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Ted Allbeury was a British author of espionage novels, many drawing on his own intelligence work.

clue.text: Austrian poet introduces realism in lyrics kindling excitement

indicators.note: introduces points to the letters that introduce, or open, each of the following words

explanation.surface: A poet from Austria brings realism into lyrics that stir excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Rainer Maria Rilke was born in Prague under the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainer Maria Rilke, author of the Duino Elegies, was an Austrian subject born in Prague.

clue.text: Friend of Violet Trefusis suggests life in Rome

definitions.meaning: ... Sackville-West had a celebrated love affair with the writer Violet Trefusis
the Latin word for life, spoken by the Romans

explanation.surface: A companion of the novelist Violet Trefusis hints at living in the Italian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Vita Sackville-West was Violet Trefusis's lover, and her name is the Latin noun for life.

clue.text: Walter with new comrade in arms acts like a father

definitions.note: the clue phrase is a verb phrase, the answer an adverb meaning in a fatherly way

parts.note: Walter Pater was the Victorian essayist and critic
an ally is a comrade in war

explanation.surface: Walter, with a fresh partner in battle, behaves in a fatherly manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Pater, the Victorian aesthete, gives PATER; the definition is loose, since the answer describes how one acts like a father.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes behaving in the manner of a parent, protective and fatherly.

clue.text: Calvinistic information to First Lady adds some points

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
Eve was the first woman in Genesis
S and E are two compass points

explanation.surface: Puritan facts given to the President's wife gain a few points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a President's wife; here it is Eve, the first woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin's church was founded in the Swiss city on Lake Leman, so its theology is called by that city's adjective.

clue.text: Waterproof lair of Stuart dramatist

parts.note: something waterproof stays dry
a den is an animal's lair

explanation.surface: The watertight hideout of a playwright from the Stuart era.
explanation.walkthrough: John Dryden wrote plays under the Stuart kings Charles II and James II.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dryden wrote plays such as All for Love in the Restoration, under the Stuart monarchy.
